header.title: Liber De Reparatione Lapsi: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Bachiarius Monachus
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp379.tmp379.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. The whole work is translated. It was chosen because no English translation of it could be found.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation of the whole work, checked against the original by a second AI only in samples. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

Footnote letters from the printed page have been omitted throughout. Line 2: the reference 'II Machab. xxi, 40' should be 12:40. Line 3: 'anis suae' read as 'artis suae'. Line 4: 'Non contradico perspicacis tuae' lacks a noun; read as 'perspicaciae tuae' (your perceptiveness). Line 5: 'Jesu magni' taken as Jeshua (Joshua) the high priest of Ezra's time; 'I Esdr.' refers to the book of Ezra.

Line 6: 'basta' read as 'hasta' (spear). The edition's reference to 1 Sam. 23:18 for the slaying of Eli's kin should be 1 Sam. 22:18. Line 7: 'spei libidinis' is probably a misreading of 'ipsam libidinis' or similar; rendered 'the very flame of lust'. 'Porca vidua' read as Dorcas (Acts 9:36-40). Line 8: the edition's 'I Reg. vii' for David and Bathsheba should be 2 Sam. 11; 'psalmo lxx' and 'Psal. lxxxii, 2' both appear for the quotation, which is Ps. 72:2 (Vulgate numbering); 'in pugna invenitis' read as 'inventus'. Line 9: 'Respice illam qui dicit' read as 'illum'; 'Elisaei illum ossa' read as 'illius'. 'B. episcopo' is an abbreviated bishop's name that could not be identified.

Evident scanning errors read silently: 'Nuntie' as 'Numquid', 'in One' as 'in fine', 'Iconis' as 'leonis', 'adsistrici' as 'assistrici', 'sermocinantur' as 'sermocinamur'. Section 10: the lament quotation ('Subleva lapides tuos super altitudines tuas') departs from the Vulgate of 2 Sam. 1:19 and is translated as given. Section 13: 'secius' (rendered 'rather') is doubtful and may be corrupt. 'Si enim ut vocatur in culpam' looks corrupt; the sense given ('is called to account as guilt') is conjectural. In the Amnon passage the logic of 'occisus est a fratre, quia...' is strained; the clause has been taken as explaining his repentance, not his death. 'confregimus' (of the lentil field, cf. 2 Sam. 23:11) is translated literally. Section 12: the reference 'III Reg. xi, 17' should probably be 11:7.

§14 'praesentiam vultus Christi': one might expect 'regis' (the king's face, cf. 2 Sam. 14:24); translated as printed. §14 'aust', 'este', 'esi', 'luam' read as ausi, est, est, tuam. §15 'pe(??)caminun' read as peccaminum; Phil. 3:17 reference corrected in sense to 3:13. §16 '(??)licam' read as Philisticam (Goliath's spear, 1 Sam. 17:7, not 22:7). 'Timet... luum' read as 'Terat... tuum' (grind, cf. Exod. 32:20); this changes the sense. 'peccatorum morum' read as peccatorum tuorum; 'spectem' as speciem; 'uveniat' as inveniat. 'fames pro gula' is obscure in a passage listing martyr's tortures; 'gula' may be corrupt for an instrument of torture. 'custodia pullicorum' read as publicorum (guards of public officers/prison); uncertain.

17: ‘Deut. xx, 7, 9’ corrected to Deut. 25:7, 9; the sentence about the spittle and the dead brother’s widow is tangled in the Latin and rendered as closely as possible. ‘Horreat consortium tuum’: the subject is unexpressed; taken as the uncharitable man described. 18: ‘Naaman Syrus’ appears to be an error for Nehemiah (cupbearer, rebuilder of Jerusalem’s walls); rendered as Nehemiah. ‘Donec’ at the start of 19 read as ‘only’ (dummodo). 19: ‘Zach. xi, 17’ corrected to Zech. 9:17. 20: verse number lost in the reference to 1 Cor. 5; it is 5:5.

21: 'luco' (grove) is read as 'loco' (place); 'cudit' as 'cadit'; 'Dirigiam' as Jedidiah (Vulg. Amabilis Domino / Ididia), which the author glosses 'in the word of the Lord'. 22: The quotation of John 15:15 reads 'filios' (sons) where the Gospel has 'friends'; the editor's Greek note is garbled in the scan. The Apocalypse reference 7:15 is probably 7:14. 23: 'obcalueris' is obscure, probably for 'occallueris' (harden); the rendering 'harden your body to bruising' is tentative.

nodes.text: THE BOOK OF BACHIARIUS TO JANUARIUS ON THE RESTORATION OF THE FALLEN
To Januarius, a brother blessed in Christ and worthy of all my faith and love, Bachiarius, a sinner, [sends] greeting.

1. Most blessed brother, I would almost have laid my hand over my mouth, stopped the pipe of my tongue, and shut the doors of my lips in silence, were I not afraid that my portion might be set among the false friends of Job, who, seeing his wound, kept unbroken silence, as though it were a wound that had no consolation. But far be it from my faith to say that there is any wound that has no consolation, when the Prophet cries out to me: Is there no physician in Gilead, or is there no balm there? (Jer. 8:22). For Gilead is interpreted 'heap of witness', and we take this heap of witness to be the whole canon of the divine books, where there is a pile of unbreakable testimonies, like a heap of stones gathered together; in this heap the true physician, our Lord Jesus Christ, is found, if he is sought. And what is the balm, if not the virtue of continence, which joins what is loosened and glues together what is torn? Knowing this, we do not hesitate to mingle the laments of our mouth with the consolation of the very wound that has occurred. For we have heard of the ruin of a dreadful disaster; we have heard of Satan exulting over the fall of a soldier of Christ; and the cheering of voices that the devil's army raised in its triumph has reached even to our ears. And I call God as witness upon my soul (2 Cor. 1:23) that my inmost parts were moved, and my bones were so shaken that I felt every part of my body tormented by the same wound. Nor would I say that this evil has happened without loss to me, when the devil's arrow has struck a member of my body, since the Apostle says: If one member suffers, all the members suffer with it (1 Cor. 12:26).

2. But my mind is not allowed to give itself wholly to lamentation or weeping, because I have reason to be angry with you. See: a brother went out with us to battle against our common enemies, and suddenly fell and was laid low. You have not judged him worthy even of the honour of burial, but have left him to be devoured by beasts and birds. Where is the mercy of the Christian religion, which our Master taught is better than sacrifice (Matt. 9:13)? See, a brother lies struck down by the enemy; perhaps he is still breathing; and you, because you are returning without a wound, have not even tried to bring consolation to his wound. Do not be without fear, most blessed brothers: the enemy struck the stronger one so that afterwards he might have quicker access to the rest. Why, I ask, do you scorn the wounded man, or do you think him dead in this way? Better was Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, the concubine of Saul (2 Sam. 21:10), who, girded with sackcloth, that is, with haircloth, guarded the bodies of the dead whom David had struck down to avenge the Gibeonites, until water dropped on them from heaven, that is, until a drop of heavenly mercy flowed down for their pardon. Better was that Judas Maccabeus (2 Macc. 12:40), who believed that prayer should be made even for his dead brothers, whom the gifts of idols stolen from the city of Jamnia had laid low.

3. Why, I ask, has our Physician placed so many kinds of remedies among the compartments of his books, if among all his plasters there is nothing by which the wound the enemy has inflicted can be healed? Was there something hidden from the Chief Physician, for which the skill of his art could make no provision? If you please, let us open the school of our Physician and search out the kinds of wounds and medicines from the beginning of the canon. See, at the very entrance of the school we meet those two authors of fleshly offspring, who, struck by the poisoned tooth of the serpent, were not at once sentenced to the everlasting punishment of death; but, cast out from the delights of paradise, that is, from the freedom of the Church and from communion in the sacred mystery, they were condemned for a time, under the figure of grief and tribulation, so that they might be healed by the poultice of penance, and might weep as exiles from the tree of life, that is, from participation in Christ, until they returned to him through the flaming sword (Gen. 3:24), that is, the fiery suffering of martyrdom, or through the Cherubim of the Lord, which is interpreted 'fullness of knowledge'. Of these there is no time now to speak one by one. And what of that fratricide, on whom the Lord ordered a sign to be put (Gen. 4:15), so that no one might kill him? For he does not will the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live (Ezek. 18:32). Not far from these is that chief of the fathers who first believed, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness (Gen. 15:6); who, taking a band of his household servants, snatched back his brother's son when he had been captured by an enemy host, and whom he afterwards delivered from the plague of Sodom, that is, from the judgement of Gehenna, by holding converse with the divine majesty, that is, by the merits of his prayer. So you too, take a band of household servants, that is, by your own work and not another's, give help to your captive brother. Speak with the Lord, that is, pray to Christ, that the fire of the judgement to come may not burn him up.

4. Imitate the deed of the patriarchs (Gen. 34:25 ff.), who not only shuddered at the violation of their sister when she fell into the hands of foreigners, but also avenged it. Ask, however, who were the avengers of the sin. Was it not Simeon and Levi? You too are of the tribe of Levi, since you serve in the Church's office. And Simeon is interpreted 'obedience'. So you, who have been obedient to God, why do you hold back from freeing or avenging a disobedient soul? Your brother's soul is your sister; if you allow her to serve among foreigners, you will sin. But perhaps you say: The one who has fallen is a Levite; the medicine of a remedy cannot be applied to him. You are wrong, brother: go back to the Physician's school. See, in the second place, that is, in the book of Exodus, where the plague and wound of the whole people is described, the Levites too are reported to have sinned; they are said to have been the first to amend at the rebuke of the lawgiver; and it is not so much the crime of sin that is charged against them as their swift conversion, in the speed of their repentance, that is praised (Exod. 32:1 ff.). Our Lord also mentions this in Ezekiel, when he says of the Levites: Who were the first to go away from me when Israel went astray (Ezek. 44:10). The high priest himself, too, made an idol at the people's urging; Moses prayed for him, that is, he was set free by a brother's help. But perhaps you say, most blessed one: The Levites had not yet been sanctified, nor the high priest consecrated, when the crime of this evil was committed. I do not contradict your perceptiveness, which you have gained from the volumes of the Scriptures. Yet I could answer you thus, according to the Apostle's statement where he speaks to the Hebrews (Heb. 7:9-10): that Levi, hidden in the loins of Abraham, both paid tithes to Melchizedek and received them. Or what does Aaron himself seem to you to have lacked of pontifical honour or rank, when he struck Egypt with dreadful signs and, going out by night with the people, celebrated the holy Passover? And we know that the Passover could not be celebrated without a priest.

5. But leaving these things aside, I want to ask you: What was Aaron when, struck with the spite of envy against Moses, he murmured together with Miriam (Num. 12:1-2)? But perhaps you will say that envy is a lesser thing than fornication. Read, then, the blessed Apostle, who says: Neither fornicators, nor the envious, nor revilers, nor the greedy, nor slanderers will obtain the kingdom of God (1 Cor. 6:9). Do you see how the things that do not enter the kingdom of heaven are joined together as equal and alike? Consider what sentence of punishment envy deserves, for which the prophetess Miriam is struck with leprosy (Num. 12:10); and greed too, for which Gehazi, Elisha's servant, is condemned to the same lot (2 Kings 5:27). Yet you, who do not loathe the greedy man, who do not shun the envious, who do not avoid the slanderer and the robber, condemn to the punishment of eternal death a brother who was for a time a fornicator and is returning? We do not say this in order to loosen the reins of sinning. Let whoever reads this note that we are not speaking to the living, but consoling a dead man. Let him only rise again, and you will see that we at once hand him the Psalmist's verse, which says: Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me (Ps. 22[23]:4). He will receive the rod of correction, and the staff that can support the weak. Let us understand the Apostle's saying, that neither the envious nor fornicators nor those who covet others' goods will possess the kingdom of God, in this way: that is, if the time of his summoning finds anyone in this vice; for elsewhere the Lord says: I will judge each one according to his ways (Ezek. 33:20). And the Apostle himself says: What they once were makes no difference to me (Gal. 2:6). In his letter the blessed John bids us pray for a brother who has not sin unto death (1 John 5:16), that is, who has not followed the evils of his sins up to the very last end of his life. Now, as for what you said above about the Levites, that they had not been sanctified when they were polluted with sins: what do you make of what is written in the books of blessed Ezra (1 Ezra 10:18), where, after the return from the Babylonian captivity, when the foundations of the Lord's temple had lately been rebuilt, not only the common people but also the priestly family, even that of the great Jeshua, are found to have mingled with foreign women, that is, with Syrians, Idumaeans, Moabites and Ammonites? Yet all of them, taking Ezra's counsel and withdrawing from the company of the foreign women, were freed from that same sin. From this you see that just as we are stained by the contagion of sin, so we are washed clean by its expulsion.

6. Let us not, I beg you, most blessed one, bury our brother under stones of despair when he has sunk into the depth of the well under the power of a wicked prince. Let us imitate that Ethiopian (Jer. 38:7, 11) who, when the holy Jeremiah had been sunk into the pit by a wicked king, took the help of thirty men, let down rags and ropes to him, and set him free. See, our brother is in the pit. Let us take thirty men, that is, either the help of the blessed Trinity, or the labour of mind, flesh and spirit, and let us free the one who has sunk into the depth of the well. Let us send him old rags: let us bring back to his memory the examples of the ancients, who fell through sin and afterwards were brought back by repentance from the depths of evils to the heights. When these have been set before his eyes, he will not be able to despair. A soldier who is struck in the first battle usually fights more bravely in the second, and rises up more angrily against the one who struck him. See, we stand at the end of the age: the battles of suffering for the name of Christ are upon us. What wonder if the one whom the spear of fornication has struck should prove the victor in the contest of suffering? What if the one whom incontinence and lust had conquered should be a victor in martyrdom? Did not that Nazirite (Judg. 16), born by promise, do just this? When a woman's blandishments had overcome him to his ruin, afterwards, at the end of his life, in the suffering of martyrdom, he is found to have laid low a greater army of enemies than before, when he was a Nazirite, that is, unstained. So too that priestly family descended from the kin of Eli (1 Sam. 3:14), to whom the Lord had sworn that none of them should stand before his face, because it had provoked the Lord with grave sins: is not that whole kindred reported to have been slain by Saul for the sake of David (1 Sam. 22:18)? And what is this but a figure of martyrdom, that those whom the grave crime of sin had entangled should be freed by a death suffered for Christ? These are the sacred mysteries of the blessed books. So the potter by no means allows his vessels to perish (Jer. 18:6), since he says he can restore them whole even when they are broken and dashed upon stones.

7. Do not spurn, I beg you, a dead brother: he is the son of the barren Shunammite woman (2 Kgs. 4:20), that is, of the Church; he who has died was born by promise. For long ago the Lord pledged and promised his birth a second time to Abraham, in the seed of Isaac (Gen. 22:15; Heb. 11:18). His head was struck by the heat at harvest, that is, the ruling part of his mind grew hot in the very flame of lust. Let his mother run to Elisha, that is, let the Church lament with anxious care: for he will rise again, if we hope for this faithfully from Christ. And you, most blessed one, imitate Elisha's work on your dead brother: lay hands on hands, feet on feet, mouth on mouth. First, so that you may suffer with him who lies dead, and not, exalted by the triumph of your own integrity, tower over him or stretch yourself above him whom sudden death has seized; but imitate the Apostle, who says: I fear lest my Lord God humble me among you, and I mourn many of those who sinned before (2 Cor. 12:21). Then set your eyes upon his eyes, so that they may no longer wander off to his ruin; [your mouth] upon his mouth, so that it may not speak wicked things; [your hands] upon his hands, so that they may not do hostile things; [your feet] upon his feet, so that they may not wander in shameful ways. And so, when your limbs have been joined to his limbs to guard him, not only will he have no further room to sin, but he will also take hope of rising again; so that he who died from the cold of sin may be called back to life by the warmth of consolation. But remember to cast everyone out of his sight: let no one see, let no one be in the midst, and let no one claim for himself the sight of him on grounds of kinship. Why do I say a kinsman? Even if it is his mother according to the flesh, let her not be given leave to enter. For you know that this is what Elisha did with the Shunammite's son (2 Kgs. 4:33), what our Lord did with the ruler's daughter (Matt. 9:25), and what blessed Peter did with the widow Dorcas (Acts 9:40). For a very secret and solitary place must be prepared for a man dead in sins, where nothing more is contained than the physician and the corpse.

8. Let us not, I beg you, most blessed one, abandon a brother who has been struck, and who was once pleasing to us, whom the enemy found unarmed. He lacked the breastplate of righteousness (Eph. 6:14; 1 Thess. 5:8), the helmet of hope and salvation, and the sword of the spirit, with which the soldiers of Christ are armed. Let him be cared for, I ask, since he still breathes; and let him return to the fight. Did not that outstanding and brave David, who in his youth overcame a giant of wondrous size, afterwards come to be overcome by the foolish nakedness of a woman? (2 Sam. 11). As soon as he recognised through the prophet's words (2 Sam. 12) that he had sinned, he at once fled to the poultice of repentance and healed the scars of his crimes by the satisfaction of confession. But not even so did the enemy cease to attack him. For afterwards too he persuaded him to sin by numbering the people (2 Sam. 24:1); and he nearly killed him by a giant's weapon (2 Sam. 21:16-17), had not Abishai, brother of Joab the commander of the army, set him free by interposing the protection of his help. Hence also, I believe, he himself says in the psalm: But my feet were almost moved (Ps. 72:2). And elsewhere: Often have they fought against me from my youth (Ps. 128:1). But you who say, 'Let there be no remembrance of him, because he has cut his own throat by a shameful sin': first inquire, brother, whether this man who fell was found in battle or was wounded at home; for the one whom an enemy struck in combat deserves more mercy than the one whom a robber stabbed while he slept. I certainly saw him standing in battle: he was fighting with the shield of fasting against the enticements of gluttony; he was fighting with the breastplate of silence against the darts of slander and the other weapons of abuse; but he was struck in the very place where he thought himself safest. For just as Asahel, the brother of Joab, David's commander of the army, who is said by Scripture to have been swift as a deer (2 Sam. 2:18, 23), on this account, I believe, that the purity of an undefiled body had granted him the gift of swiftness (for the body which is corrupted weighs down the soul, Wis. 9:15), is reported to have been struck in the loins with the point of the spear by Abner, whom he was pursuing. That the vice of fornication is located in this part of the body, I think no one doubts. Just as Abner himself is said afterwards to have been struck in the groin by Joab, Asahel's brother (2 Sam. 3:27); because the figure of fornication deserved to be slain nowhere but in the groin. But did Asahel lack the consolation of his brothers, when the whole army of David lamented him so? Or was he blotted out of the book of life, that is, from the memory of the Lord's reading? Scripture does not forget him in this way, so that it even mentions the swiftness he had before his death, when it says: He was swift as a deer; that is, he not only avoided the snares of the enemy by the keenness of his mind, but also proved a slayer of serpents, that is, of the adverse powers.

9. Remember, brother, that we are flesh: that sea (that is, the form of baptism) which blessed John says in the Apocalypse that he saw, he described as being of glass (Rev. 4:6; 15:2); and therefore in us it is quickly endangered or broken. The way of this world is slippery, bound fast by icy wickedness: when the heat of desire has thawed it a little, it easily leads to the fall and ruin of the wretched. Stretch out your hand to your fallen brother (Sir. 15:18), who, confounded by the shame of his sin, dares neither to raise himself nor to lift up his eyes. Fulfil the law of Moses: If the ass of your brother has fallen under its load (Exod. 23:5), that is, the flesh overcome by sin, bend down, humble yourself, and lift it up from its fall. Why do you blush to be joined to a sinful man? Look to him who says: Do not be overly righteous (Eccl. 7:17). Our Master not only judges the man wounded by robbers (Luke 10:30) worthy of care, but also restores him to his inn and fold; and, having given the innkeeper two denarii, that is, the two Testaments of the divine canon, he promises him a greater reward if by his diligence he brings the stricken man back to his former state. So you too, gather up your brother, whom the robber devil struck with the band of his henchmen: entrust him to the innkeeper, that is, to Bishop B., who, if he spends anything on him, will receive more from the Lord. But perhaps you say: That man was wounded; this one is dead. Then you too, if you call him dead, at least place him beside the bones of that Elisha (2 Kgs. 13:21). I do not want you to separate him far from the members of Christ, because he will blush at the company of better men and will rise again to life. Do not think it a small torment of correction if a sinner is admitted into the company of the blessed; for he feels their rewards to be his own torments. If someone is praised, he blushes; if someone is rebuked, he recognises himself. Placed among these lashes of words, he draws ever nearer to satisfaction and amendment.

10. Now what kind of thing is this, which we have heard some people say: that the woman and the man who are partners in the crime and sin should be joined as if in matrimony and wedlock? Far be this from the speech of a Christian mouth. This is the serpent's suggestion: that he should take up even the corpse of the one he has killed. Is it not the same as if someone gravely wounded were gasping at the very end, and an earthly physician, if he happened to visit him, were to urge that he be killed, because he suspects he cannot live? Without doubt what is said here is the same: a brother or a sister has been found gravely wounded by the dart of lust. When the marriage of his crime is urged on this person, what else is said but 'Let him be killed, because he cannot live or escape from this wound'? Perhaps you do not know what punishment awaits the one who despairs? When that messenger of Saul's death (2 Sam. 1:2 ff.) came to David and reported to him that his enemy had been laid low, David, asking the cause of death, heard from him that the messenger himself had killed him with his own sword, adding and saying: Because I saw that from the blow of the wound dealt to him he was not going to live (ibid. 10). David at once condemned him to death, because he had despaired that a man struck by enemies would live, and had cut his throat, taking away the confidence of hope. Rather, after David's manner, let the garments of the heart and breast be torn; let a tearful voice be raised in lament; let the people of Israel, that is, the people of the Church, be taught the lament, and let them say: Raise your stones upon your heights, and think of your slain, how the mighty have fallen in battle. Let it not be announced in Gath, nor proclaimed in the streets of Ashkelon, lest the daughters of the foreigners rejoice and the sons of the uncircumcised exult (ibid. 19, 20), and the rest that is contained in the decree of that lament. And let one say or speak: See, it is forbidden that the fall or ruin of a brother be spread within the borders of Gath or in the territory of Ashkelon, that is, to the knowledge of secular or worldly men; and have we allowed not only the very city he lives in, but the whole world, to be filled with despair over his reputation? Does not that saying of the Gospel also agree with this precept, which says: If your brother sins against you, rebuke him alone; if he listens to you, you have gained him; but if he does not listen to you, take with you two or three witnesses (Matt. 18:15, 16), and the rest that the saying of the precept contains? You see, then, what it says: Lest the sons of the uncircumcised exult. Wretched me, who know these things! For who are the sons of the uncircumcised but the men of this world, living in the error of their sin and in heathenism? These, then, exult when they hear of the ruin of a soldier of Christ, or console themselves by his deed, saying: Look at the one who was held up to us in reproach by the others, by whose example we were urged to live; who, though he had sprung from our own body, yet was said, to our confusion, to have a life unlike ours. Would it not have been better not to begin what is good than to fall so shamefully, or not to be able to complete what you have begun? They do not know that at the judgement of God the soul which is known to have willed the good and to have been tripped up by the one lying in wait will perhaps have a greater excuse than the soul which, rebellious against God, out of the despair of slavish fear, chose rather to be handed over to the yoke of captivity than to face the danger of the contest. Is not a soldier excused before his king by his own wounds, and does not the mark of his scars often commend a vigorous fighter?

11. But leaving these things aside, let the dead man be mourned, let the dead man be buried; that is, partly by our labour, partly by the confusion of his own shame, let his sin be hidden and taken out of the midst. Let us provide the linen cloths of consolation and the spices of heavenly hope; and let him, within the tomb of his own seclusion, confounded by the shame of sin, keep himself shut in; there let him be torn by the worm of his own conscience, which may consume all the rottenness of sins in him, until he gives off from himself no stench of shameful reputation. Did not blessed Tobit in this way earn the pardon of heavenly mercy, by giving burial to his brothers who died in captivity? — I believe, by urging and instilling repentance in those who had fallen under the dominion of the prince of the world (Tob. 1:18; 2:9). So let us too cover his body, as he deserves. See, a prophet went out from Jerusalem (1 Kgs. 13:1 ff.), that is, from the house of the Lord, against Bethel, which was committing fornication away from the Lord, that is, the city of this world; the Lord had commanded him not to taste of its food or drink. But he who was deceived by the wicked one through a false prophet, that is, through the spirit of fornication, fell into the power and lot of the lion, which goes about roaring, seeking whom it may devour (1 Pet. 5:8). Yet it stood beside his corpse, so that unless it were carried to the bosom and tomb of the Church, it would serve it as food and meat. But let us at least imitate the office of the false prophet, and bury the one whom the devil has struck with the honour owed to all. Christ is accustomed to raise the dead from such a tomb; only let us not leave his corpse to be devoured by beasts or birds, that is, by vices or by men of the world. How, I ask, can we despair of the mercy of the Lord, who even rebukes Pharaoh for not deigning to repent at all, saying in the prophecy concerning Pharaoh: I have broken the arms of the king of Egypt; and he did not pray that healing might be given in him and strength restored to him to grasp the sword (Ezek. 30:25)?

12. That wonderful Solomon, who was found worthy to be united with the one who sits beside God (Wis. 9:4), that is, Wisdom, fell into the embraces of foreign women; and, ensnared by the chain of lust, he also defiled himself with the error of sacrilege, when he made an image to Chemosh, the idol of Moab (1 Kgs. 11:7). But he who acknowledged the guilt of his error through a prophet, is he an exile from heavenly mercy? But perhaps you say: You nowhere read in the canon that he repented or obtained mercy. Listen, then, brother. His repentance, which is not written in the public scriptures, some may perhaps say was acceptable for this very reason, that he repented not before the face of the people, but in the secret of his conscience, with God as witness. And we know that he obtained pardon from this: that when he had been released from the body, Scripture records that he was buried among the bodies of the kings of Israel; which, however, we know was denied elsewhere to sinful kings who remained in the perversity of their purpose to the end of their life. And therefore, since he was found worthy to be buried among the righteous kings, he was not a stranger to pardon; and pardon itself he could not have earned without repentance. As for that company of Korah: although for the rashness of their daring it was swallowed alive by the opening of the earth, yet we are commanded by the Lord to have their censers, in which they lit strange fire, placed around the altar (Num. 16:37), because they are said to have been sanctified. These we take to be their souls, in which they had received the heat of an adulterous flame with presumptuous licence; and so they are swallowed alive, but their censers are forbidden to perish; as the Apostle also says: I have handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ (1 Cor. 5:5). Consider, then, brother, how few are granted to free their limbs, unstained by the bite of sin, from the amphitheatre of this world, where the fight is with beasts, that is, with vices. He who had experienced this said: Do not hand over to the beasts the souls that confess to you (Ps. 73:19). But since we have now been conversing with you for a long time, we must take care that our wordiness does not offend you. Therefore we turn our pen also to you, for whose sake we have said these things.

13. Why do you flee from me, brother? Why do you entrust yourself rather to the company of worldly men? They perhaps laugh at your fault; I lament it, and if it be necessary to die with you, I shall wish it. Why do you blush at our presence? Our case is like yours, because I too am confounded with shame in your affair. The Ammonite king, as I see (2 Sam. 10:4 ff.), shaved off half the beard of David's soldiers, that is, of the ministers of Christ, and cut off their tunics as far as the groin: that is, by taking half their beard he took from them the appearance of men, and he is shown to have made them effeminate through the razor of pleasurable vices. Half your beard has been shaved, because by one vice you have lost whatever good you had done in the virtues of God; and you are shaved of half your beard, because if you are willing to labour in the remaining time of your life that is left to you, it will grow again. And he cut off their tunics as far as the groin when he revealed before the eyes of men the shameful deeds which he himself had prompted. But even beyond this there is hope. Let us stay in Jericho until our beards grow: that is, let us be the reproach and disgrace of better men and become a thing accursed to all, as Jericho was to the people of Israel, until the appearance of beards, that is, the growth of virtues, springs up in us. Believe me, our king will grieve at the injury; he will avenge us his soldiers, to whom the enemy did these things to dishonour him. Our king David was absent from our sight for a little while; and therefore, overcome by enemies, we have broken down the part of the field full of red lentils, which is the figure of our modesty and delicate chastity. But now that our king has opened the remembrance of sin to the eyes of our heart, let us stand firm, so that at least what is left, that is, the remaining time of our life, may be defended and kept safe. Do not, I beg, let anyone persuade you, whoever he is that tells you to turn this rather into wedlock and call the crime a marriage. I do not want you to provoke and multiply God's offence. For if what the enemy persuaded you to do secretly and with fear is called to account as guilt, how will it deserve pardon when you begin to claim it for yourself publicly, as if mocking God and his judgement? Imitate that Amnon, son of David (2 Sam. 13:15 ff.), who, after he had burned with an unlawful flame to violate his sister, afterwards hated her more than he had loved her before; and he was killed by his brother for this deed — [yet], having recognised the guilt of his error, he did not remain in the crime, but vehemently hated the very matter of the sin. Hence we also suspect that David was not moved against him, because he soon saw that he had taken up repentance, and that he at once hated with impatience that by which he had been deceived for the space of one hour, and by the power of repentance broke its snares. But he who is caught in the net of vices and patiently submits to his enemies, that is, to the hunters, until he is even shut up in a cage and there fattened for a long time for the show — he will be most pleasing to the princes of the world when he has been killed. Until you have escaped the mousetrap of fornication, do not trust yourself to the snares of drunkenness, through which you may run into the anger of an enraged Absalom (ibid. 28); for lust and drunkenness have a kind of brotherhood with each other in the birth of vices.

14. Lift up your spirits, then, brother, raise the eyes that the shame of conscience has bowed down, and do not let hostile despair break you. See, Absalom, who had killed his brother, earned the king's pardon through the intercession of friends (2 Sam. 14:23), so that he did not even despair of asking for the kiss of peace and the presence of the face of Christ. You too, then, be humble and bowed before those whom you know to be friends of David, who was once your father, when you had not sinned, so that what you cannot gain by yourself you may earn through their intercession. And if they happen to be hard of hearing, do not cease to beg in season and out of season; for Absalom gained by injury what he could not obtain by friendship, and what he did not earn by his merits he obtained by injury. Do you want to know that the saints often pray for sinners on the occasion of an injury? That blessed one of the four, head of confessors and martyrs, when he was pressed with stones by a frenzied people, at the very going out of Israel from Egypt (Ps. 105:1), that is, of the soul departing from the body, knelt and besought the Father for sinners (Acts 7:59), following the example of our Master, who asked pardon for the people persecuting him (Luke 23:34). See, you observe how the occasion for prayers arises from the injury and suffering of the saints. We do not say this so that you may earn the intercession of the blessed by insulting them; but we give this counsel, that if, because of the greatness of your crime, they have not dared to plead, then, bearing the injury of your persistence, they may more readily be heard on behalf of the one by whom they were wronged. Set fire to the barley next to you, which is in the field (2 Sam. 14:30); for the tongue is a fire (Jas. 3:6), and the field is this world. So whenever you begin to disparage the fruits of a good life and to say: 'See what sort of saints these are, who do not dare to ask for sinners: where is the daily reward of their work?', then the hope of the saints, set on fire by your tongue, will be stirred to confidence in interceding; for they will recognise that you were driven to this necessity for the sake of your own benefit, not by the vice of detraction. Just so Absalom did not burn Joab's crop because he wished to harm him as an enemy, but so that he might at least in this way turn his attention to the one disparaging him, whom he had not listened to when he was flattering; and so that he might thus earn the presence of the one who was the neighbour or friend of Christ. For the fruit of the saints that is according to men is not unfittingly understood as barley, while that which is according to God may be reckoned as wheat; for there is no doubt that the saints sow both, according to the Apostle, providing good things not only before God but also before men (Rom. 12:17). And so Absalom burned the barley next to him, that is, the way of life carried on among men; but he could not reach that which is before God, because the Father alone has known it.

15. But perhaps you will say: 'Your persuasion requires a quiet or secure man; but I must daily fear a persecutor from the world, who wishes to avenge on me the disgrace of his kinswoman.' If, then, you are afraid of something of this kind, see, there are six cities of refuge (Josh. 20:2ff.); enter them, if you please. And if perhaps, because of your consciousness of sins, you do not dare to enter those that are in the land of promise, that is, in the Church, there is Bezer beyond the Jordan in the wilderness, which is interpreted 'narrowness', that is, the small or modest cell of a monastery; and it will suit you very well, because it is of the lot of Reuben, and he unlawfully defiled his father's bed (Gen. 49:4). There is also Ramoth of the lot of Gad, which is interpreted 'lofty death' or 'vision of death'. For truly repentance should be called a lofty death, when, with his members mortified, a man is led to the heights of heaven from which he had previously slipped down; or else, beside this lowly death which hangs over all flesh in general, that [death] is reasonably named lofty by comparison with it, because it is far nobler to die through repentance than to be dissolved by this common death. If, however, we wish to understand 'vision of death', it can be taken thus: when we are set in repentance and place before our eyes the torments of Gehenna and hell, we see the very form of the death from which we are freed by the benefit of repentance. Only remember that you are doing penance in the city of the handmaid's son; for Everyone who sins is a slave of sin (John 8:34); and taking the form of a slave, you must humble yourself even to death (Phil. 2:7–8). There is Golan in the territory of Manasseh, which is interpreted 'rolling', so that you may remember that you must roll in sackcloth and ashes; and this in the territory of Manasseh, which is interpreted 'forgetfulness', so that, forgetting the things you did before, you may stretch forward to what lies ahead (Phil. 3:13). Dwell here, then, so that through narrowness, death and rolling you may escape the persecutor's anger and find hope of salvation. Then afterwards, if you have done anything profitable in these, you will be able to reach even Kedesh in the land of promise, which is in Galilee, which is interpreted 'holy'; so that when in tribulation you have cast off the work of corruption, access may be granted you even to the holy Church; and to the lot of Naphtali, which is called 'a vine let loose' (Gen. 49:21), so that you may be worthy to share in the sacrament of the Lord's blood. Nor let the way into Hebron be closed to you, which is interpreted 'joining' or 'marriage'. For let your soul return to her husband, that is, to the Spirit of God, of whom she had for a time been widowed by sins. And so you will be able to enter also the sixth city, Shechem, which our Joseph obtains as an inheritance, because he was buried there; which is interpreted 'shoulder' or 'labour', so that you may show that through the labour of repentance you have been carried back from your straying on the shoulders of Christ (Luke 15:4–5), and joined to the ninety-nine sheep, and made the hundredth; for that same Shechem is written to have been bought from foreigners for a hundred lambs (Gen. 33:19).

16. But why, brother, does torpor still delight you as you lie there? Rise, for the Physician has come, who says that the rottenness of sins must be cut away, and after that the wound of the scar itself must be treated. Why are you terrified? Why do you flee the cure? You who were not at all afraid of the Philistine spear, weighed down with a weight of six hundred shekels (1 Sam. 17:7), why do you shrink from the little knives of the Gospel's surgical iron? You who endured the fire and flames of the enemy, why do you fear the fire of the Lord, the one he came to cast on the earth (Luke 12:49), which will consume hay and stubble and wood (1 Cor. 3:12)? Cut away from yourself the rotten will of habit; burn your kidneys and your heart; condemn the hostile beauty of your body, through which you were either deceived yourself or deceived others. Let your emptied limbs shudder with fasting, and accustom yourself to have as your covering the sackcloth which you had defiled for a filthy purpose, so that when you are pricked by its touch and roughness you may always remember the goads of your sins. Let Moses grind up in you your calf (Exod. 32:20), through which you ran riot in the wilderness; that is, let the discipline of the law and of fasting wear down your flesh, so that, reduced to nothing, it may be made thin. You have read, I believe: Be angry, and do not sin (Ps. 4:5). So you too be angry at your sins, so that you sin no more. Anticipate the cruel torments of avenging Gehenna, and become your own torturer, so that when the enemy comes he may find nothing in you that he can punish. If an occasion of martyrdom comes, remember how you must fight in the presence of your King, so that you can amend the guilt of a deserter and runaway. But if perhaps the occasion of this happiness is lacking, you can be your own persecutor, so that, as the Apostle said (Rom. 12:1), you may present yourself to God through every death. Enter the prison of your monastery, and seek out the darkness of solitude by which you may be called back to the light you lost. Let hunger take the place of the gullet, and thirst the place of the flame, so that by the hand of your will as executioner, through the punishment of abstinence, the framework of your ribs may be stripped of flesh, and, in place of the torment of fire, the burning of harsh thirst may feed on the inner marrow of your bones. Let your vigil be like the watch kept by public officers; and, bound by a harder habit and rule as by a chain of rigid iron, await, in the likeness of martyrdom, the pardon of heavenly mercy. Come, come, why do you hesitate? That ladder of Jacob (Gen. 28:12), from which you fell, is still set up and not yet withdrawn, if you are willing to climb; and although in your fall you have bruised all your limbs, still try again to climb, and until you come to that rung from which you fell, keep and guard yourself firmly; for although every ascent is slippery, that one quickly tips you over and throws you down into the depths.

17. But perhaps you may say that, in the manner of the Pharisees, I lay heavy burdens on men’s shoulders and am myself unwilling to touch them with my finger (Matt. 23:4). See, brother, since licence to swear is forbidden us (Matt. 5:37), if you put any trust in my unhappy self, I pledge, according to the mercy of the Lord, that I am willing to be a sharer in this labour which I urge; and, desiring your salvation, I do not merely press my companionship on you, but offer it; and if perhaps you are ashamed to come to us, send word, and I will hurry without delay to bring you. Let him shrink from your companionship, as from Ruth from the land of Moab, that is, of a soul coming from drunkenness and fornication, who seeks only his own things and, ignorant of mercy, glories only in his Israelite stock. But I, though I am not like Boaz (Ruth 4:1 ff.), still desire your soul to be joined to me; and let no one charge me with presumption, for it is lawful for me to raise up seed from the widow of a dead brother (Deut. 25:7, 9), so that I may not lose the paschal sandals and be made disinherited of Christ’s passion; and, made as though blind in respect of the bridegroom’s word, so that I may not receive the spittle of a fasting mouth that is spat on the ground and trodden underfoot, until, having poured out seed, I go in to the widowed soul of the dead brother, that is, of one dead through despair; but, having sought out an abundance of seed, having gathered from the Scriptures a wealth of words, I may be joined to this widow and draw near, so that, having heard these things, she may conceive without difficulty and bring forth the spirit of salvation. For I remember the words of the apostolic precept, where he says: ‘Snatch some from the fire, but console the doubtful’ (1 Thess. 5:14); and elsewhere: ‘He who calls back a sinner from the error of his way will save his soul from death’ (James 5:20). It is no small thing if we pull the tip or top of an ear from the lion’s jaws (Amos 3:12); although I think that the most blessed bishop, who in those same parts stands at the divine altar with his priests, does nothing other than imitate the work of David: that when a lion or a bear has snatched a sheep from the flock, he rises against it, and, having throttled its jaws, tears the prey from its throat; or like a good shepherd calls back the wandering, binds up the bruised, and turns back the straying.

18. You, however, brother, must by no means acquiesce in a wicked and unchaste marriage: do not insult Him whose wrath you will not be able to endure. Rather, let her too whom the guilt of crime made your partner return to her husband. Is the sister of the patriarchs (Gen. 34), after she sinned, said to have married? The Lawgiver commanded (Lev. 20:10) that whoever defiled another’s wife should be stoned together with her; and so he does not permit marriage, but under the name of stones a harsh sentence amends and corrects the sin. Look at the prophet, who says: ‘And I said, after you had played the harlot, return to me’ (Jer. 3:1). Although the Assyrian king seized the vessels of the Lord’s temple (Jer. 27:16), still let them return to the temple (1 Esd. 1:7–11), so that unclean Babylon may not possess them for ever. Although through the flame of shameful lust the chief of the cooks, who prepares for his master, that is, the prince of the world, dishes of our sins, has set fire to the temple of the Lord, yet let Zerubbabel come, that is, the spirit of wisdom, who has already understood that the power of women rules over evil men, and trusts wholly in truth; let Ezra come, the library of the Law and the memory of reading; let Nehemiah the Syrian come, the strength of confidence and despiser of fear, who for the rebuilding of his homeland does not fear the power of the prince; and, having posted throughout the several places of Jerusalem (2 Esd. 4:16–17), that is, the members of the body, the angelic and patriarchal virtues, so that what has collapsed may be rebuilt and he may guard what has been rebuilt, let him serve the building with one hand and the guard with the other; for Adam was placed in paradise to work and to guard (Gen. 2:15). Let, then, the barriers of the gates be rebuilt through the tropologies of the names. Let the Sheep Gate be rebuilt first (2 Esd. 3:1, following the Septuagint), which we suppose to be hearing, through which we test whether the things that come in to us from outside are good or bad; for faith is from hearing (Rom. 10:17). Let us do what the Apostle says: ‘If you are in the faith, test yourselves’ (2 Cor. 13:5). Let the Fish Gate be rebuilt (2 Esd. 3:3), that is, the ever-roving nature of our sight, and the swift and fleeting glance of the eyes along the paths of the sea, that is, the ways of this world; for sight itself may be reckoned a dragnet: whatever it looks at, it at once catches, and what it has caught it sends on to the inner storerooms of the heart. Let the gate in Anathoth be rebuilt, which is interpreted ‘answering sign’ (ibid., 6), which we suppose to be the crossbeam of the forehead, where we have received the sign of our salvation and of the Lord’s holiness: this is the golden plate on which the high priest is commanded to receive the name of the Lord written, the tetragrammaton. Do you want to know that we not unfittingly take the gate in Anathoth, which is interpreted ‘answering sign’, for the crossbeam of the forehead? The prophet joins to this gate the places of the perfumers (ibid., 8), which through the tropologies of the names are said to have been rebuilt by other virtues. And what are the places of the perfumers, if not those which are touched by the sanctification of chrism? After these follows the Gate of Fruit (ibid., 13), which we suppose to be the office of the mouth and of taste, through which the fruit of all seeds, that is, of the words of God, goes forth. Let the Dung Gate also be rebuilt (ibid., 14), which we suppose to be the entrance of the nostrils or of smell, through which shameful allurement deceived us, and we reckoned as gain what was dung (Phil. 3:8). Let the Strong Gate also be rebuilt (2 Esd. 3:15), which I believe to be the office of our hands or of touch; for we did not hold strongly what we held, and another took our crown (Rev. 3:11). Let the walls of the Pool also be rebuilt (2 Esd. 3:15), that is, the form of our baptism and the broken defences of the mystic font, which are the marks of chastity; for when the wall of continence was breached by lust, as though the barriers of the sacred water had burst, we poured out and lost the water of the font. Its walls are said to be rebuilt for this reason, that we may know the mercy of the Lord to be so great that even the times of broken chastity can be rebuilt and called back to their former likeness by the virtue of continence. So you too should understand, through the words of the names and the tropologies of the places, that these things said to be rebuilt are the offices of the members.

19. Only do not imitate the deed of the king of Babylon (Dan. 5:2 ff.), so as to think you ought to drink the wine of perdition from the bowls of the Lord’s temple, and that before your gods, Venus, Mars and Mercury, that is, fornication, or avarice, or rage; for it is written: ‘The rage of man is incontinent’ (Job 31:11, following the Septuagint), and elsewhere: ‘Avarice, which is idolatry’ (Eph. 5:5). For you cannot reckon avarice to lie only in money; for avarice is felt above all in lust, on which no limit is ever placed. That virgins are called bowls in the temple of the Lord, the Prophet teaches us, saying: ‘Wheat for the young men, and sweet-smelling wine for the virgins’ (Zech. 9:17, according to the Septuagint); and if wine is poured into something, what should it be called but a bowl? I should indeed like to be taught by the more learned by what authority of Scripture a corrupted woman is urged to marry, when blessed David did not allow even his concubines, whom his son defiled by shameful intercourse, to marry afterwards or have husbands (2 Sam. 20:3). Did he not keep them as widows to the end, providing them with sustenance? David, that is, the Lord Christ, does not want his wife to be had by another man in his sight. Then too that daughter of Saul (2 Sam. 3:13 ff.), whom he had lost for a time during persecution, he afterwards demanded to be given back and restored to him; and although she had been joined to another as well, still she is taken from him and assigned to the one whose she had been before. You have defiled David’s wife: do not presume this any further; but, as the man who had taken her did, weeping and mourning, give her back and restore her.

20. And perhaps that one wiser than all the beasts, the ancient counsellor (Gen. 3:1), has suggested to you that you could do this penance which we urge on you in your old age, and now satisfy the hunger of your desire under the name of marriage. But do not quench with the moisture of vices the gospel spark that comes from that fire of the whole book, where it says: ‘Fool, this night your soul will be demanded of you’ (Luke 12:20). For if among those whose marriages are honourable they cannot last long, how will they endure with you, where they are joined with crime? Let him come who says that this crime is to be amended by marriage, and that a marriage is to be named from so great a wickedness. For marriage is a word of religious meaning (Heb. 13:4), since it is granted with God as its author. See, the Apostle cries to honourable marriages: ‘Having, as though not having’ (1 Cor. 7:29). And who says, ‘Let the adulterer have, use, practise’? But I see what he turns to in his own defence; for it is written, he says, ‘It is better to marry than to burn’ (ibid., 9). This was said of a virgin or a widow. This woman is no longer a virgin. Then she was burning, and she married; now let her cool, and live. She is not a virgin, because she has been corrupted; she is not a widow, because her husband lives for ever. Why then do you urge marriage on her? Do you want to know what the Apostle’s judgement is on this error? He says in his Epistle: ‘It is actually reported that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not found even among the gentiles, so that someone has his father’s wife’ (1 Cor. 5:1). See, something similar was done. This young woman who sinned was the wife of the Father, of that Father who begot us by the word of truth (James 1:18). She was joined to him in marriage, I believe, at the time when, after the example of Rebecca coming from Mesopotamia to Isaac, she received the veil with which to cover her head (Gen. 24:65). Of this deed the Apostle says: ‘I have handed such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved’ (1 Cor. 5:5). Did he say, ‘I have ordered him to marry her whom he corrupted’? No, but ‘I have handed him over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.’ For Satan is interpreted ‘adversary’; by which, I believe, he means that the flesh which sinned should feel whatever is adverse to its pleasures, whatever is adverse to its will, so that the spirit may be saved in the day of our Lord Jesus Christ.

21. But you too, brother, should curse whoever has urged this on you. For see: animals worn out with age are never slaughtered in the sacrifices; everywhere it is either a lamb, or a calf, or a he-goat, or a kid that is offered (Exod. 29 and elsewhere), that is, sins still tender and small, or slight. In one place only do we read that Elijah offered a bull, and that only once (1 Kgs 18:33). This was permitted to the Saviour alone, who slaughtered the inveterate sins of the whole people. But do not think that your sin is still a tender kid. Believe me, it is a he-goat. See through how many tracts of land your stench, that is, the report of your shameful reputation, has travelled. How then can what stinks so much not be called a he-goat? The Prophet says that he is blessed who takes the little ones of Babylon and dashes them against the rock (Ps. 136:9). And are you waiting until your enemy becomes a giant? But if you want to know, it is a giant already. For as soon as the sons of God desired the daughters of men, giants were born from them (Gen. 6:4); for the giant's form is huge beyond measure, beyond the stature of other sins. And if perhaps there is someone who says that David also took the woman with whom he had committed adultery into the partnership of marriage (2 Sam. 11:27), the case is not alike: for she was the wife of a king, but that one the wife of a soldier. He, being an earthly man, could be killed by the scheming of a crafty plot; but this King is heavenly, whose wife has been corrupted and violated. Nor does the suffering of death come near him in any way, for he is not temporal but eternal. And yet David did not presume to take Bathsheba to bed while Uriah the Hittite was present, though he was his own soldier, though an earthly man. Did he not try not only to press it on him but even to force it from him (ibid. 13), that after the food and drink which by a crafty plot he had ordered to be served to him in abundance, he should lie down in his own house and bed? How will you claim for yourself the bed of an adulteress while her husband is alive and present, and at the same time a King, which is greater than these, immortal and everlasting? But perhaps you will say: ‘When the cause of the defilement was known, her husband cast her off and rejected her.’ You deceive yourself, brother, for he himself proclaims through the Prophet: ‘What is the bill of divorce of your mother, by which I sent her away?’ (Isa. 50:1). And elsewhere: ‘Shall he who falls not rise again? Or he who turns away not turn back? Why does my people not repent of its wickedness, and, held fast in their evil purpose, they would not return to me?’ (Jer. 8:4–5). See, the prophet by the Lord’s command took a harlot as wife (Hos. 1:2 ff.); and do you say that a soul has been cast off by God to perdition? Nor do I myself speak against this marriage, if you can beget from this union such fruit as came forth from Bathsheba and David, whom the Lord through the prophet named Jedidiah, that is, ‘in the word of the Lord’ (2 Sam. 12:25), who among men was called Solomon, that is, ‘Peaceful’, and held the rule of the whole world, that is, of the whole man. Such a son is born of penitence; such a son do the groans and laments of mourners bring to birth. Then too blessed David himself, though in his youth he was caught with an adulteress, in his old age is found with a virgin (1 Kgs 1:1 ff.); so that we may understand that after sin long chastity is an imitator of virginity. So you too should imitate David, so that her whom you had as companion in the vice of corruption you may have as partner in the labour of penitence: not that you should do penance joined together, but that, separated from one another, you may be joined by doing one work; for a brand still smoking from the fire is quickly caught by the devouring flame.

22. Above all, then, brother, let no hostile despair grow in you because that faithless man asserts that the fallen cannot be restored; for the Lord says: ‘All sins and blasphemies will be forgiven men; but whoever sins against the Spirit, it will not be forgiven him’ (Matt. 12:31). But I say that this very thing, to despair of the Lord, is to sin against the Spirit, for the Lord is Spirit (John 4:24); and it is not forgiven him for this reason, that he did not believe that the Lord could give back to him what he lost. For what is there that will stand in the way of our pardon? Our Lord is almighty. Is it impossible for the almighty to blot out sin? Our Lord is good; for no one is good but God alone (Luke 18:19). Can this fault fall upon that surpassing and perfect goodness, that he should not hear one who prays to him? Come then, friend, rise up; and having lost your wages and substance amid the waves of the world, like a shipwrecked man hold fast to one plank (Luke 15:13), that is, to the knowledge of the divine canon, which may bring you to the shore, where it says: ‘If his sons forsake my law and do not walk in my judgements, if they profane my ordinances and do not keep my commandments, I will visit their iniquities with the rod and their sins with stripes; but my mercy I will not scatter from them, nor will I do harm in my truth’ (Ps. 88:31–34). Of whose sons is this said? Is it not of the sons of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom the womb of the Church’s font and the matrix of a secret and intricate mystery brought to birth; whom, once born, the cradle of the Cross received and the breast of the Gospel suckled? Do you want to know also that the baptized, not the catechumens, are called sons? See what he himself said to his Apostles: ‘No longer will I call you servants, but sons’ (John 15:15). So you too, if you know that you were a son, that is, if you had something apostolic in you, are not permitted to despair even so. But if you have always performed the office of a servant, that is, of a sinner, let greater boldness be given you to rise up: for the fall of one who slips from a low place is lighter; and he who, having always been engaged in error, at some point turns himself to an upright life is weighed down by a lesser burden of wrath than those who, after holy deeds, have lived shamefully and sewn an old patch onto a new garment (Mark 2:21). And what of what he says to his Churches in the Apocalypse, which among the number of the faithful are compared to seven-branched lampstands under angelic guard? ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and do your former works: otherwise I am coming to you soon, and will remove your lampstand’ (Rev. 2:5). And in an earlier part of the book he says he saw a countless people (Rev. 7:15), who in tribulation washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; whom, he says, the Lamb of God leads to the springs of life (ibid. 17). Yet we take this to be the number of the penitent, since they were saved only through tribulation and mourning.

23. So you too, wash your robe in the spring of tears: perhaps you will be able to imitate the fine linen of chastity. What if he grants you purple, and you pour out the juice of your blood for his name? And scarlet you will have in abundance, if you blush at the things you did before. Nor will you lack blue, if you harden your body to bruising and bring it into subjection (1 Cor. 9:27). And so with these colours you may perhaps at some time be woven into the tabernacle of the Lord. This, dearest brother, compelled by love and grief for you, I have attempted even beyond my strength and ability. You will have a double punishment on the day of judgement if, like deaf asps, you spurn the words of our charm (Ps. 57:5); or if you think fit to despise either the word of one who entreats, or the counsel of one who warns, or the feeling of one who grieves. May Jesus Christ, the Son of God, restore to you twofold your goods taken from you through the envy of the devil; and may you be so reconciled to the Lord that you may deserve to intercede also for us, who are your friends, in our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.
